segments.text: Let's talk about hospitality. The real thing, not the industry, the craft.
I want to start with a distinction that changed the way I think about this work.
There is a difference between service and hospitality. Service is technical.
The food arrives hot. The room is clean. The check-in takes five minutes.
Service is measurable, and it's mandatory. We must be excellent at it.
But hospitality is something else. Hospitality is how the guest feels.
Service happens to the guest. Hospitality happens inside the guest.
You can have perfect service and zero hospitality.
We've all been to those hotels, flawless, polished, cold as a hospital corridor.
And you can have humble service with overwhelming hospitality.
Think of your grandmother's house.
The tablecloths might not be pressed, but nobody in history has ever felt unwelcome
at their grandmother's table. Craveral has to be both, the standards of a
great hotel and the feeling of a home.
Our welcome should say what our brand says, Fica. Pertence.
Stay, belong. So how do we do that, concretely?
First, guests are guests, not customers. The word matters.
A customer is someone in a transaction. A guest is someone in your home.
When friends come to your house, you don't process them.
You open the door, you're happy to see them, you offer them something to drink.
You make them feel that their arrival improved your day. That's the posture.
Every arrival, every day, including the day you're tired, including the arrival at
22 hours when you wanted to go home.
That family drove two and a half hours from Lisbon Airport, probably with children
asleep in the back seat. Their holiday starts with your face.
Second, use names. From the reservation, from the check-in, learn
them. "Welcome back, Mrs. Keller.
How was the beach?" Costs nothing and is worth everything.
People spend their whole lives wanting to be recognized.
In a world of apps and QR codes and self-service kiosks, a person who remembers
your name is becoming a luxury. We will always offer that luxury.
Third, anticipate. The deepest hospitality answers needs the guest hasn't voiced
yet. It's cold tonight. Are the fire pits lit before someone asks?
A couple booked the owner's house for an anniversary.
Is there something waiting for them that says we noticed?
A child at dinner is melting down. Can we bring the pizza a little faster without
being asked? Watch, notice, act.
Anticipation is just attention plus initiative, and both are free.
Fourth, know the land, tell the land.
Every one of you should be able to tell a guest where to watch the sunset.
Which beach suits small children?
Carvalhal, by the way, easiest access, and our beach bar is right there.
Where the fisherman's trail is most beautiful, what medronho is, and why they
should try it. You are not staff who happen to be in Alentejo.
You are the guest's connection to this territory.
That's the belong gesture, remember. Bring those who eat closer to those who grow.
Every conversation is a chance to make that connection.
Fifth, the small rituals matter more than the grand gestures.
Guests forget the marble lobby of some five-star palace within a week.
What they remember for years, the waiter who remembered which wine they liked on
the second night, the housekeeper who arranged the child's stuffed animals on the
pillow, the receptionist who printed the boarding passes without being asked twice.
Hospitality is compound interest.
Tiny deposits made consistently that add up to a feeling of being cared for.
Let me tell you what I consider the perfect Craveral moment.
A guest once told me at checkout, and I've never forgotten it, she said,
"Pedro, the strangest thing happened to me here.
On the third day, I stopped taking photographs."
I asked her what she meant, and she said, "I realized I wasn't trying to prove I
was here. I was just here." That's it. That's the whole job.
Everything we do, the silence we protect at night, the walkways through the trees,
the food from 80 meters away, the fact that nobody is pushing an activity schedule
at anyone, all of it is engineered to help a human being arrive.
Not just check in, arrive in the deepest sense of the word.
Our guests live in cities under pressure on screens.
We give them back the rhythm of the land, sunrise, work, food, rest, stars.
When it works, it's not a holiday, it's a repair.
And you, whatever your role, you're a guardian of that repair.
The housekeeper who works quietly while a guest sleeps late is protecting it.
The gardener who waves good morning is part of it.
The waiter who doesn't rush the table under the stars is honoring it.
One last thing for this model. Warmth is not servility. We are warm.
We are generous. We are attentive. And we carry ourselves with dignity always.
You are professionals in one of the most meaningful crafts there is, taking care of
human beings. Walk like it. Never grovel, never be cold.
Between those two extremes lives everything I mean by the word hospitality.
Next model, the guest journey. From the first click to the last look in the
rearview mirror.
